title: Hard Tech Is Now One-Fifth of a YC Batch: Software Companies Are Being Eaten by Agents
dek: In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the work done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.
why: This episode is an insider using batch data to talk trends, with concrete numbers and cases on both the hard tech and agent lines. High information density, good for quickly calibrating your judgment.
who: For people watching hard tech, AI agents and early-stage investing, especially founders and investors who want to read the direction of YC batches and are considering building hard tech or agent products.
skip: The chit-chat and encouragement at the end, from 33:22 to 36:28, is low density and can be skipped.

points.body: Diana analyzed companies YC admitted over the last 18 to 12 months: hard tech's share rose from 8% to 20%. Broken out: robotics from 1% to 6-7%, industrial manufacturing from 4% to 10%, defense from 1.5% to 5%, semiconductors and photonics from 1% to nearly 4%, power infrastructure from 1% to nearly 3%. Across the physical atom stack these numbers generally tripled to quintupled. Over the same period, the median YC company had zero revenue when admitted; in past batches median monthly revenue was about 8K by demo day, now it's 20K.

points.h: The share of technical founders is rising
points.body: Jared mentioned that in the current summer batch, one in every six founders has a PhD, far above historical levels. The reason is that working on things like silicon photonics usually requires a strong research background. Gary added that hard tech used to be hard because supply chains and software engineering were the limiting factors; now with codegen, a top-tier full-stack hardware company no longer needs to hire a thousand great engineers — one or two people, or a small team, is enough, and that changes the economics. The real bull case isn't that investors are avoiding software, it's that the models themselves are accelerating scientific research, letting startups make research breakthroughs earlier.

points.h: Defense and space became the new narrative
points.body: Gary said three macro trends are driving atom growth. First, after SpaceX's successful IPO, a generation of founders wants to build space companies, like Exosat doing sovereign Starlink solutions and Beyond Reach Labs doing satellite solar panels. Second, this generation of founders grew up in an environment where war was heavily discussed, and they want to do defense. Icarus builds a solar-powered U-2 reconnaissance aircraft that can do surveillance and communications, and has already landed a seven-figure contract with the new Department of War; Nine Mothers builds counter-drone defense, a shotgun turret with CV, and special forces are buying it. Third, compute itself is a heavy physical process: the cost of an A100 per hour is rising because demand is too great and supply too short.

points.h: Hardware companies are growing at software speed
points.body: Nox Metals is bringing metal manufacturing back to the US, rebuilding the metal supply chain in empty Detroit factories. Its customers are emerging defense tech companies that need metal to build things, and existing suppliers are mostly slow-moving old businesses that can't keep up with the pace of new defense companies. Gary analogized to the early Web 2.0 era: new startups prefer to buy from new startups because they can collaborate at the same speed, like using Stripe instead of a traditional credit card provider. PG tweeted that Nox Metals is growing at software speed.

points.h: The compute stack digs from chips down to power
points.body: Diana said GPU prices are anomalous: the A100 is already old, yet its cost per hour is still rising because demand exceeds supply. Around data center bring-up — site selection and construction, software, the actual buildout, power solutions — there are startups working at every layer. Further down to core compute silicon: Lamb Labs is building a new processor, Bot is building a new custom hardware architecture using ternary representation, because as Nvidia went from A100 to H100 to B300, floating-point precision dropped generation by generation, and LLM architectures don't need full-precision floating point — even FP2 can work. Dipole Labs is building all-optical switches, because electronic switches can't keep up with GPUs and have become the bottleneck in many data centers.

points.h: Systems of record either get eaten or become the harness
points.body: Gary's argument: if you're a system of record, you either get raided — once you ship an MCP, the data moat disappears and switching becomes easy — or you become the harness yourself, the place where people don't just read and write but actually get work done. He cited the RKGI benchmark: the same model plugged into different harnesses performs differently; model plus harness is what equals output. Some claim Astra with a custom harness exceeds 90% on RKGI 3, when a few months ago that number was in the low double digits.

points.h: The share of software doing complete tasks doubled
points.body: Diana said the share of YC-admitted companies doing full-stack end-to-end tasks rose from 10% to over 25%. The difference is that agents actually do the work, rather than being point solutions that still need a human to operate them, like SaaS five to eight years ago. The fastest-growing ones are exactly these companies doing complete workflows, such as insurance brokerage, clinical intake, medical billing. Jared added that it's been nearly a year since agentic coding became truly usable (Opus 4.5), and these workflows are now blooming across the board; people are willing to pay more for software that "gets the work done."

points.h: Zero to seven-figure revenue in three months
points.body: Diana said that this year, for the first time, she saw companies go from zero to seven-figure revenue during the batch, over a span of just three months; in the past this took 18 months or more. Part of the reason is that they're solving real problems, and agentic coding raises product maturity — founders can run 20 coding agent sessions at once. Another fast-growing category is selling data or RL environments to labs, and many of these companies keep a low profile. Over the past two years YC has invested in more than a dozen companies with annual revenue over $10 million selling data or RL environments, many reaching hundreds of millions, with the companies only a few years old.

terms.def: The software layer that wraps a model and lets it actually execute tasks; model plus harness is what equals output.
Simulated or real interactive environments used to train models with reinforcement learning; a data category labs pay for.
Using AI to automatically generate code, reducing hardware companies' dependence on large numbers of software engineers.
The system in an enterprise that records core data, like Salesforce or Slack; its moat comes from accumulated data.
Physical-world data collected from a robot's or person's own viewpoint, used to train robot models.
